panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A shows the T1-weighted MRI of the brain with a nodular mass characterized by concentric alternating signal intensity layers, consistent with Baló concentric sclerosis, as described in the text (Figure 2A). B: Panel B shows the T2-weighted MRI of the brain with the same nodular mass demonstrating concentric alternating signal intensity layers, supporting the diagnosis of Baló concentric sclerosis (Figure 2B). C: Panel C displays the FLAIR-weighted MRI, showing the lesion demonstrating alternating signal intensity layers, though less prominently than on T1 and T2 sequences, consistent with Baló concentric sclerosis (Figure 2C).
panels.attribution_text: Di Dier and Lemmerling. Baló Concentric Sclerosis.. Journal of the Belgian Society of Radiology 2022. doi:10.5334/jbsr.2914. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
in_text_mentions: gnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination of the brain, a nodular mass was demonstrated in the left frontal lobe, characterized by concentric alternating signal intensity layers on the T1- and T2-weighted images (Figure 2A–2B, respectively), and less prominently on fat-suppressed FLAIR-weighted images (Figure 2C). No locoregional mass effect nor surrounding edema were seen. The outer border of the lesion moderately enhanced after intravenous injection of gadolinium (Figure 3). No other contrast enhancing lesions were identified. The diagnosis of active Baló concentric sclerosis was concluded.

c sclerosis has a typical appearance on MRI. Concentric low to iso-intense layers are observed on T1-weighted images. That layering pattern is iso- to hyperintense on T2-weighted images. These imaging findings are well demonstrated in Figure 2. Active demyelination is marked by contrast enhancement, typically located in the peripheral ring of the lesion as shown in this case in Figure 3. In an early stage these findings only occur on MRI, making it the imaging modality of choice. In a later disease stadium, the typical layering pattern may vanish. Diagnosis should then be made with biopsy [1].

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a sagittal T2-weighted MRI clearly showing the characteristic hyperintense concentric onion-like pattern in the right parieto-frontal area, consistent with Balé's concentric sclerosis. B: Panel B is an axial T2-weighted MRI demonstrating the hyperintense concentric onion-like mass in the right parieto-frontal area, supporting the diagnosis of Balé's concentric sclerosis. C: Panel C is an axial FLAIR MRI showing the hyperintense concentric pattern within the lesion, which aligns with the definition of Balé's concentric sclerosis. D: Panel D is a coronal post-contrast T1-weighted image of the lesion showing open ring enhancement, which is a known radiological finding in the context of Balé's concentric sclerosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows serial brain MRI findings (T1, T2, FLAIR) demonstrating demyelination-like signal abnormalities, which is consistent with the clinical presentation of Balo's concentric sclerosis described in the caption and article context. B: Panel B shows gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealing pathognomonic 'onion-bulb' concentric ring-like enhancing lesions, supporting the diagnosis of Balo's concentric sclerosis.
panels.attribution_text: Li et al. Case Report: Beyond the monophasic myth: relapsing Baló's concentric sclerosis with residual disability.. Frontiers in human neuroscience 2026. doi:10.3389/fnhum.2026.1794003. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Serial brain MRI findings. (A) Axial T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and FLAIR sequences demonstrated demyelination-like signal abnormalities in the right centrum semiovale and left parietal lobe. White arrows indicate the core demyelinating lesions. (B) Gadolinium-enhanced coronal, axial, and sagittal T1-weighted images revealed characteristic “onion-bulb” concentric ring-like enhancing lesions, featuring alternating T2/FLAIR hyperintense-isointense rings (consistent with the “fried egg” sign in Balo’s concentric sclerosis). White arrows indicate the pathognomonic concentric ring lesions.
in_text_mentions: Brain MRI performed on day 6 showed suggestive demyelinating lesions. A subsequent enhanced MRI on day 8 demonstrated the definitive “onion-bulb” appearance—concentric T2/FLAIR rings with characteristic concentric ring-like enhancement (Figure 1), confirming BCS diagnosis.

in_text_mentions: CT of the brain showed a well-defined, hypo-dense round lesion (~1.3 cm) with possible mild mass effect in the right corona radiata. The brain MRI revealed the lesion had T2/flair hyperintense signal with a bullseye appearance, concerning for BCS (Figure 1). Cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine MRIs were negative. The patient was diagnosed with BCS by exclusion by the neurology and internal medicine teams.

panels.figure_caption: Additional MRI brain images. Axial T2 FLAIR images through the pons (A), midbrain (B), and cerebrum (C) demonstrate scattered supra- and infratentorial subcortical and deep white matter hyperintensities involving the left middle cerebellar peduncle, right ventral pons, left anterior temporal lobe, and right frontal and parietal lobes (arrows). A sagittal post-contrast T1-weighted image (D) shows periventricular hypointense lesions consistent with classic "Dawson’s fingers" (arrowhead). FLAIR: fluid-attenuated inversion recovery.
in_text_mentions: MRI of the brain (Figures 2, 3) demonstrated a lesion with diffusion restriction, T2 hyperintensity, and heterogeneous open ring enhancement on post-contrast T1 imaging. The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map revealed a distinctive layered ‘onion peel’ pattern, which is characteristic of BCS.

plate_findings.evidence: Numerous T2-hyperintense white matter lesions within the subcortical periventricular deep white matter and corpus callosum.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A displays extensive T2 hyperintense white matter lesions, which are part of the manifestation of Balo concentric sclerosis. B: Panel B explicitly shows the hallmark finding of Balo concentric sclerosis: a concentric bullseye area in the left parietal lobe. C: Panel C shows an enhancing lesion consistent with Balo concentric sclerosis in the temporal lobe. D: Panel D shows an enhancing lesion consistent with Balo concentric sclerosis in the temporal lobe.
panels.attribution_text: Al Ashi et al. A Rare Case of Balo Concentric Sclerosis, a Subtype of Tumefactive Multiple Sclerosis, in a 40-Year-Old Male: Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.24033. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A-D): MRI brain with and without contrast. Figure 1A shows numerous T2-hyperintense white matter lesions within the subcortical periventricular deep white matter and corpus callosum. Figure 1B shows a concentric bullseye area of T1 isointense and low-signal intensity seen in the left parietal lobe with surrounding vasogenic edema and enhancement measuring 2.1 cm X 1.8 cm X 1.6 cm. Figures 1C and 1D show a smaller enhancing lesion in the left posterior temporal lobe, demonstrating wispy enhancement from an axial and coronal view. Several lesions demonstrate low T1-signal intensity/black holes. There was no intracranial hemorrhage, mass lesion, or acute infarct. There was no extra-axial fluid collection or hydrocephalus.
in_text_mentions: s identified on T1 MRI in the left parietal lobe with surrounding edema vasogenic ring enhancement measuring 2.1 cm X 1.8 cm X 1.6 cm, which was consistent with BCS superimposed on MS, seen in Figure 1. On MR spectroscopy, a sequence of incomplete ring-enhancing lesions demonstrates lactate peak and increased choline non-specific, which is consistent with BCS. MRI of the cervical spine showed questionable high T2-signal lesions in the spinal cord at the level of C5-C6.
